title: LLM trading agents find decent entries but struggle with exits—any advice?
author: SnooCapers9097
selftext:
I’ve set up LLM trading agents backed by quant engines and have been testing the setup for over a month with different agents and brokers.  
They’re configured for scalping or day trading, with different strategies and sector focuses to keep risk down.  
The biggest issue so far is sell signals. They seem to find decent entries, but the exits aren’t great—they hold too long or miss opportunities to take profits.  
For anyone working with automated trading systems, how do you handle exits? Do you use fixed take-profit and stop-loss rules, trailing stops, time-based exits, or let the model decide based on updated signals?  
Any advice or lessons from your own testing would be highly appreciated.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: exits are where the LLM hurts, because "hold or sell" gets re-asked every bar and the model keeps finding a reason to hold. I'd take that call away from it: the model picks the entry, and a stop, a target and a time stop get fixed in code at the fill. Quantradin, a thing I built, grades exactly that on real fills, free. quantradin.com. do your agents get re-prompted every bar?

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: For scalping and day trading, I would keep the LLM out of the hard exit path initially. Replay the month of entries through several predeclared policies, fixed stop/target, trailing stop, time exit, and signal reversal, using each broker’s actual spread, latency, and fees. Compare expectancy, drawdown, profit giveback from peak, and time in trade by strategy and sector. Then let the model choose only among those bounded policies at entry. If it can revise exits continuously, it may simply rationalize holding losers or moving targets after the fact.

replies.author: SnooCapers9097
replies.body: Thank you 🙏 let me test it out.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Exits are often better as fixed rules in code than left to the model, because an LLM tends to hold on when the story still sounds good. Something like an ATR-based stop, a trailing stop and a time stop, with the model only allowed to tighten them. I haven't run these agents myself, but I'd test a few exit rules on the same entries and compare how much of each trade's peak profit gets given back. Cymetica's Backtest Labs is one place to compare exit rules on the same history.

comments.author: MycoHost01
comments.body: Have a fixed exit or just no exit just let it run and see where all trades average out and use that as the fixed exit so if all trades reach more than 10% do that!

comments.author: Frodo_Baghodler
comments.body: Great question. My AI sucks at this too, so you're not alone!

comments.author: Technical-Athlete-9
comments.body: If the LLM can figure out the setup in real time then it should be able to explain the rules or tell you what additional inputs might clarify it. Get the data, program the rules, backtest, profit.
